Mode: **create** — first plan for q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Step 1 survey — what the tree already records:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): Birth ~1845, **Ireland** (F1, citing S1 the 1850 census, dwelling 84) — the project objective says Pennsylvania but the tree's documented source says Ireland; the 1870 search will record whichever birthplace Patrick gives and may resolve this.
- Patrick Flynn (I1): Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (F2, citing S3, death cert no. 4521) — death already documented, no separate search needed.
- Thomas Flynn (I2): Birth ~1818, Ireland (F3, unsourced); no death fact; no spouse recorded.
- Relationship R1 (Thomas → Patrick): Cited quality 2 from 1850 census (S1), 1860 census (S2), and death certificate (S3) — all are indirect or secondary, inferred from household co-residence and death-cert reporting.
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is listed in the tree's sources but not cited by any fact or relationship — not yet searched or extracted.
- Patrick's mother is entirely absent from the tree.

**Plan: pl_002 (q_001), 9 items**

- **pli_004** (seq 1) — fs_hints, Schuylkill County PA, 1845-1908, FamilySearch: Review pending FamilySearch hints on Patrick Flynn (I1; FamilySearch PID not recorded in project tree — look up before executing) before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

- **pli_005** (seq 2) — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/), name-searchable: The researcher specifically requested this. The tree holds 1850 (S1) and 1860 (S2) census entries placing Patrick in Thomas's household; the 1870 census extends the record ten years closer to Thomas's presumed death and may for the first time show his wife — Patrick's mother, entirely absent from the tree. Patrick (~25) may appear in Thomas's household or nearby. Search Flynn and variant Flinn.

- **pli_006** (seq 3) — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, FamilySearch, collection 1438024, name-searchable; **fallback for pli_005**: Independent indexing of the same year at no cost; cross-check if Ancestry yields nothing.

- **pli_007** (seq 4) — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, FamilySearch, collection 1417683, name-searchable: The first census with an explicit relationship-to-head column; if Thomas (~62) is still alive, the link to Patrick would be stated directly rather than inferred from household position. Also records father's and mother's birthplaces — could point to the Irish county of origin needed for baptism research.

- **pli_008** (seq 5) — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1840-1895, FamilySearch, SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable: **Dedicated parents' marriage item.** A marriage record for Thomas Flynn and his wife confirms the couple, supplies the mother's maiden name, and by its date corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father. Per loc_001, Schuylkill County parishes remained under the Diocese of Philadelphia throughout this period. Caution: the marriage may have occurred in Ireland before the post-famine emigration; if nothing is found here, Irish registers are the next recourse. The marriage alone does not prove Patrick is their child; that still requires a record placing him with both parents.

- **pli_009** (seq 6) — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1845-1880, FamilySearch, SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable: Search for baptisms of Patrick and any siblings listed under Thomas Flynn's parentage. Siblings born after the family's arrival (~post-1848) could appear in Schuylkill County registers; a baptism entry naming both parents is direct parentage evidence and would strengthen the case for Patrick's family membership. Per loc_001 quirk, some coal-region church films are browse-only image groups — if name search fails, browse the parish register images.

- **pli_010** (seq 7) — probate, Schuylkill County PA, 1860-1895, FamilySearch, collection 1999196, browse-only (personCount 0): S4 is in the tree sources but not cited anywhere — not yet extracted. Thomas Flynn (~born 1818, last seen in S2 the 1860 census) could have died 1860-1895 — his lifespan sets this window. A will naming Patrick as a son would be the most direct parentage evidence available; an intestate administration listing heirs may also name the mother. Browse the Schuylkill County probate docket volumes for Flynn entries in this range.

- **pli_011** (seq 8) — military, United States, 1861-1865, FamilySearch, collection 1910717, name-searchable: Patrick (~16-20 at the war's outset) may have enlisted; a compiled service record or pension application could name next of kin — possibly Thomas as father or the mother's name — providing a secondary derivative source corroborating parentage.

- **pli_012** (seq 9) — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1850-1870, FamilySearch (FAN — required for parentage, BCG Standard 14): For each census year Thomas appears (S1 dwelling 84, S2 dwelling 112, and the 1870 search), review the surrounding enumeration district entries for other Flynn/Flinn households. Irish immigrants in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region commonly settled near kin from the same home townland; a neighboring sibling's household composition may reveal Thomas's wife's surname or the family's county of Irish origin — evidence bearing on Patrick's parentage that no record of Thomas alone can supply.

Fallback relationship: pli_006 executes if pli_005 (Ancestry 1870) yields nothing usable.

entry.rationale: The 1860 census (collection 1473181, name-searchable) should show Thomas Flynn (~42) as head of household with Patrick (~15) listed as a child and, critically, Thomas's wife — Patrick's mother — by name, age, and birthplace. The 1860 census is already cited in the tree (S2, on the Thomas–Patrick parentage relationship at R1) but was never formally extracted through the research workflow: no assertions or log entries cover it. A household listing Thomas, his wife, and Patrick together corroborates the co-enumeration claim and reveals the mother's given name, estimated birth year, and birthplace. Siblings born before 1860 would appear here too with birthplaces (Ireland or Pennsylvania), helping to fix when the family emigrated. Search under Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania; also try variant spellings Flinn and Flyn.

Patrick's Pennsylvania death certificate (cert. no. 4521, 12 March 1908) is already in the tree (S3) and is cited on the Thomas–Patrick parentage relationship at quality 2 (secondary evidence), indicating an informant stated Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father. Formal extraction through the research workflow has not been done — no research.json assertion covers it. The PA Death Certificates collection (2255317) is name-searchable (personCount 4,218,763). The informant who provided the death information may have named both parents, including the mother's given name and maiden name, and their birthplaces. This is also the subject's own death entry: Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland, where the birth parish is the unknown being sought, so his own death record is the next best statement of origin facts after the birth register itself. Search under Patrick Flynn, death year 1908, Schuylkill County.

The 1870 census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) should show Patrick (~25) either in Thomas's household or in his own nearby household. If Thomas (~52) is still alive, the household listing will again show Patrick co-resident. If Patrick is in his own household, the census records his birthplace (Ireland) and occupation. Search under Patrick Flynn and Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County; also check adjacent Northumberland, Carbon, and Columbia counties in the anthracite region, where Irish coal miners commonly relocated. Variant spellings: Flinn, Flyn.

The 1880 census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) introduced explicit relationship-to-head labels for every household member — the first federal census to do so. Patrick (~35) appearing as 'son' in Thomas's household is stronger parentage evidence than the 1850 co-enumeration alone. Thomas (~62) may still be living; if so, each household member's relationship to him is stated. If Patrick is in his own household, the 1880 schedule records the birthplace of each person's father and mother in dedicated columns — those entries directly state Patrick's parents' origins. Search under Patrick Flynn and Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County, PA.

The 1900 census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) is the only federal census schedule that asks each respondent to state the birthplace of their father AND the birthplace of their mother in separate columns. Patrick (~55) should be in Schuylkill County; Thomas (~82) is likely deceased by 1900 (born ~1818). Even if Patrick reports only birthplaces rather than names, 'Ireland' for both parents directly corroborates the Thomas Flynn hypothesis and may prompt further Irish-records research. If siblings appear in nearby households, they can be searched separately for more specific parentage evidence.

A will or letters of administration for Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as an heir would be direct parentage evidence. Thomas was born ~1818 in Ireland; his plausible death range in Schuylkill County is 1860–1905 (ages 42–87), and Thomas's plausible lifespan sets this window's bounds. The Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 collection (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 (Schuylkill County probate, 1851–1930) is also browse-only (recordSearchablePercent 0). The tree registers S4 ('Schuylkill County Probate Records') as a source but no assertions have been extracted from it; this item initiates that formal browse. The loc_001 locality entry notes that probate is held by the county Register of Wills and is a primary parentage source naming heirs. Browse the docket index under Flynn / Flinn / Flyn, then pull the will or administration file.

A dedicated search for the parents' marriage is required on every parentage plan. Thomas Flynn (~born 1818) and his wife married before Patrick's ~1845 birth, placing the event roughly 1835–1848 (Thomas aged 17–30); Thomas's plausible age at marriage sets this window's bounds. The PA Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, name-searchable) and PA Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, name-searchable) both cover this period; search under Thomas Flynn. The marriage record (a) confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple before Patrick's birth; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which census and death records usually omit; and (c) corroborates the parentage by dating the union before Patrick's birth. Important limit: the couple's marriage proves only that they married — it does not place Patrick in their household and is not by itself evidence that he is their child. A record placing Patrick with Thomas and his wife (a census household or a baptism naming them as parents) is still required. If no PA marriage is found, the marriage likely occurred in Ireland before emigration and is out of scope for this plan; the mother's maiden name would then need to come from other sources.

Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland and has no Pennsylvania baptism; however, any younger siblings born in Pennsylvania after the family's emigration would have baptism records in the Catholic parishes of the anthracite coal region, each naming Thomas and his wife as parents — direct parentage evidence for Patrick through sibling corroboration. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, personCount 982,415), covering 1708–1985, is the first search. Search under Thomas Flynn and, once the mother's given name is known from item 1 or 7, under her name as well, for baptism entries of children born 1847–1875. The loc_001 entry notes Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese level and that Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (later Allentown from 1961). Godparents named in baptism entries are FAN evidence — often siblings, cousins, or trusted community members — and may lead to further Flynn family records.

Fallback for item 8: if the name-searchable SYNTH-PA-CHURCH search returns nothing for the Flynn family, browse image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842–1895, browse-only, recordSearchablePercent 0). The loc_001 entry notes that some church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only (image-by-image). The volume includes English- and German-language registers; Catholic registers may be in Latin. Browse chronologically for the likely years of sibling baptisms within the 1847–1875 window.

Irish immigrants to the anthracite coal region typically sought naturalization within years of arrival. A declaration of intent or petition for naturalization for Thomas Flynn would record his name, age, birthplace, date of emigration, and — in later petitions — his wife's name and children by name and age. A petition naming Patrick as a child is direct parentage evidence. Image group 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849–1915) is browse-only (recordSearchablePercent 0). Browse the volume's index for Thomas Flynn / Flinn / Flyn; this item's date range is 1849–1880 (Thomas's plausible naturalization window: he appears in Schuylkill County by 1850 and was born ~1818, making him 31–62 in that window). The witnesses named in the petition are FAN members — often relatives or community members — a secondary yield that may identify other Flynn family connections.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Here is the research plan the agent produced for **q_001 — Who were the parents of Katharina Seeger (b. c. 1843, Baiersbronn)?**

---

## What's already in the tree

Katharina Seeger (I1) has only one recorded fact: birth "about 1843" in Baiersbronn, Württemberg. No parents, no spouse, no children, no sources, and no FamilySearch ID are on file.

---

## Key finding: all records are on Archion

FamilySearch holds **no indexed collections and no digitised image volumes** for Baiersbronn. All Protestant parish registers for Baiersbronn (baptisms, marriages, burials, and the Familienregister) are digitised exclusively on **Archion**, a paid German church-archive platform.

Parish page: https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn

---

## Plan pl_001 — 4 items, all on Archion

| # | What to look for | Date range | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **pli_001** | **Familienregister** (household/family register) | 1800–1875 | Groups both parents and all children on one page — the most efficient single source for 19th-century Württemberg parentage. Search for any Seeger/Seger/Säger household with a Katharina born c. 1843. |
| **pli_002** | **Baptism register** — Katharina's own entry | 1840–1847 | A baptism entry directly names the father and mother. Check surname variants (Seeger, Seger, Säger). |
| **pli_003** | **Marriage register** — parents' marriage | 1815–1843 | Confirms the couple, gives the mother's full maiden name, corroborates the father's identity. (Note: this alone doesn't prove Katharina is their child — pli_001 or pli_002 does that.) |
| **pli_004** | **Siblings' baptisms + godparents** (while browsing pli_002) | 1820–1870 | Note every sibling born to the same Seeger parents; record all godparents — frequently relatives, they supply leads to associated families. Best done in the same Archion session as pli_002. |

---

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: The 1880 U.S. Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) is the first census to record each person's relationship to the head of household, so co-residence of Patrick and Thomas Flynn in 1880 would state 'son' directly rather than requiring inference from position and shared surname as in the 1850 and 1860 entries. Thomas (born ca. 1818) would be approximately 62; Patrick (born ca. 1845) would be approximately 35 and likely heading his own household — but searching Thomas Flynn's 1880 household identifies any remaining children and confirms whether Thomas is still alive, narrowing the date window for the browse-only probate search (item 5). Patrick's own 1880 household entry records his parents' birthplaces. Variant spellings Flynn, Flyn, Flinn, and Flyne should be checked.

A parentage plan requires a dedicated search for the parents' marriage record. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) covers 1708-1985. Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother would name the wife's maiden name — which no record found to date has supplied — confirming the couple as a unit and opening surname-based searches for the mother's own records and for sibling christenings (item 3). The locality entry notes Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875); sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese. Date range: Thomas (born ca. 1818) could have married 1835-1855 for a child born ca. 1845. Note: this record confirms the couple married; it does not by itself establish that Patrick is their child — that link requires a record placing him with them.

Christening and baptism entries for Patrick Flynn and his siblings (other children visible in the 1850 and 1860 census households of Thomas Flynn) name both parents in each entry — the church baptism register is the standard original record for parentage in this era and community. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable. Any child's baptism naming Thomas Flynn and his wife provides direct evidence of parentage for that child and is corroborating FAN evidence for Patrick's parentage; a sibling's baptism entry naming Thomas as father is an independent source from the same family circle. The mother's maiden name recovered from item 2 (Thomas's marriage record) will guide the surname search here. Date range covers when Thomas and his wife's children would have been born and baptized.

Patrick Flynn (born ca. 1845) would likely have married in Schuylkill County between roughly 1865 and 1895. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable. Roman Catholic marriage registers frequently recorded the groom's father's name and parish of origin, which would be direct evidence naming Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father. A marriage entry also states Patrick's age and birthplace — corroborating or resolving the Ireland/Pennsylvania birthplace conflict between the census entries and the death certificate. The 1908 death certificate informant was James Brown, identified as son-in-law; his daughter's marriage record to Patrick is therefore a high-priority target and may name Thomas Flynn in the groom's entry.

Thomas Flynn's will or estate administration is the highest-probability single FAN source for direct evidence naming Patrick as a son. The locality entry confirms Schuylkill County probate records are held by the Register of Wills (available from 1811). Collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994) returned browse-only (personCount 0) — browse the county docket images for 1860-1910, the span from Thomas's last confirmed census appearance to the outer limit of his plausible death. Date range is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan: born ca. 1818 Ireland, last seen in 1860 census, could realistically have died 1861-1910. Results from the 1880 census search (item 1) will help narrow this window before the browse begins. A will naming Patrick as son, or an administration bond listing Patrick as an heir, is direct parentage evidence independent of the census-based inferences.

The 1870 U.S. Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) was not searched in either prior plan. Patrick would be approximately 25 in 1870 and may still appear in Thomas Flynn's household or in an adjacent one. Thomas (approximately 52 in 1870) should be traceable if alive; if he cannot be found in 1870 it narrows his death to 1861-1870. Finding them both in 1870 fills the census gap between 1860 and 1880, identifies remaining siblings in the household, and extends the chain of co-residence evidence before the 1880 census relationship column becomes available. Variant spellings Flynn, Flyn, Flinn, and Flyne should be checked.

Deeds, mortgages, and other land transactions involving Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County name witnesses and boundary-adjoining landowners — his FAN cluster. Boundary recitals in deeds explicitly identify the owners of adjoining parcels, who are frequently kin or close neighbors in immigrant communities of this era. A conveyance from Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn would be direct evidence of a father-son relationship. If Thomas transferred property near the end of his life, the deed or a subsequent administration transfer may name his heirs. Witnesses to deeds often appear repeatedly across transactions and can extend the FAN network. The Schuylkill County courthouse holds originals; FamilySearch may have digitized deed books for this period.

Patrick Flynn (born ca. 1845) would have been 16-20 years old during the Civil War (1861-1865). If he served in the Union Army, his compiled service record and pension file (Civil War Soldiers Index, collection 1910717, name-searchable) would contain extensive personal information: birthplace, age at enlistment, and — in a pension application — the names of parents or next of kin, siblings, and witnesses who could attest to his identity and family history. A pension deposition naming Thomas Flynn as his father would be independent corroborating evidence of parentage from a federal record, drawn from a context entirely separate from the census and death-certificate chain. Variant spellings should be checked.

Patrick was born in Ireland ca. 1845 and appears in Pennsylvania by the 1850 census, meaning the Flynn family immigrated ca. 1845-1850 during the Famine emigration. FamilySearch ship passenger manifests for this period are name-searchable. Famine-era manifests frequently list family groups traveling together, naming the head and accompanying family members with ages. A manifest listing Thomas Flynn with children of matching ages — including one consistent with Patrick — would be FAN evidence of the family unit from before the 1850 census, predating the Pennsylvania co-residence that forms the current chain of inference. Ports of Philadelphia, New York, and Boston all handled significant Irish Famine immigration. Variant spellings Flynn, Flyn, Flinn, and Flyne should be checked.

Other children of Thomas Flynn visible in the 1850 and 1860 census households would have death certificates — if they died after Pennsylvania's 1906 civil registration — naming Thomas Flynn as their father. These are independent FAN-corroborating sources: siblings' death certificates naming the same father strengthen the parentage case through separate informants who may have known Thomas Flynn personally or been present at Patrick's birth. The informants on siblings' death certificates (spouses, their own children) likely had firsthand knowledge of Thomas Flynn, making them stronger secondary sources than Patrick's son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at Patrick's birth. Date range set by the siblings' plausible lifespans: children born ca. 1840-1860 to Thomas Flynn (born ca. 1818) could realistically have died 1906-1950. Sibling names can be drawn from the 1850 and 1860 census household listings and from any christening records found in item 3.

items.rationale: The 1880 U.S. Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) is the first census to record each person's relationship to the head of household, so co-residence of Patrick and Thomas Flynn in 1880 would state 'son' directly rather than requiring inference from position and shared surname as in the 1850 and 1860 entries. Thomas (born ca. 1818) would be approximately 62; Patrick (born ca. 1845) would be approximately 35 and likely heading his own household — but searching Thomas Flynn's 1880 household identifies any remaining children and confirms whether Thomas is still alive, narrowing the date window for the browse-only probate search (item 5). Patrick's own 1880 household entry records his parents' birthplaces. Variant spellings Flynn, Flyn, Flinn, and Flyne should be checked.

A parentage plan requires a dedicated search for the parents' marriage record. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) covers 1708-1985. Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother would name the wife's maiden name — which no record found to date has supplied — confirming the couple as a unit and opening surname-based searches for the mother's own records and for sibling christenings (item 3). The locality entry notes Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875); sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese. Date range: Thomas (born ca. 1818) could have married 1835-1855 for a child born ca. 1845. Note: this record confirms the couple married; it does not by itself establish that Patrick is their child — that link requires a record placing him with them.

Christening and baptism entries for Patrick Flynn and his siblings (other children visible in the 1850 and 1860 census households of Thomas Flynn) name both parents in each entry — the church baptism register is the standard original record for parentage in this era and community. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable. Any child's baptism naming Thomas Flynn and his wife provides direct evidence of parentage for that child and is corroborating FAN evidence for Patrick's parentage; a sibling's baptism entry naming Thomas as father is an independent source from the same family circle. The mother's maiden name recovered from item 2 (Thomas's marriage record) will guide the surname search here. Date range covers when Thomas and his wife's children would have been born and baptized.

Patrick Flynn (born ca. 1845) would likely have married in Schuylkill County between roughly 1865 and 1895. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable. Roman Catholic marriage registers frequently recorded the groom's father's name and parish of origin, which would be direct evidence naming Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father. A marriage entry also states Patrick's age and birthplace — corroborating or resolving the Ireland/Pennsylvania birthplace conflict between the census entries and the death certificate. The 1908 death certificate informant was James Brown, identified as son-in-law; his daughter's marriage record to Patrick is therefore a high-priority target and may name Thomas Flynn in the groom's entry.

Thomas Flynn's will or estate administration is the highest-probability single FAN source for direct evidence naming Patrick as a son. The locality entry confirms Schuylkill County probate records are held by the Register of Wills (available from 1811). Collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994) returned browse-only (personCount 0) — browse the county docket images for 1860-1910, the span from Thomas's last confirmed census appearance to the outer limit of his plausible death. Date range is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan: born ca. 1818 Ireland, last seen in 1860 census, could realistically have died 1861-1910. Results from the 1880 census search (item 1) will help narrow this window before the browse begins. A will naming Patrick as son, or an administration bond listing Patrick as an heir, is direct parentage evidence independent of the census-based inferences.

The 1870 U.S. Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) was not searched in either prior plan. Patrick would be approximately 25 in 1870 and may still appear in Thomas Flynn's household or in an adjacent one. Thomas (approximately 52 in 1870) should be traceable if alive; if he cannot be found in 1870 it narrows his death to 1861-1870. Finding them both in 1870 fills the census gap between 1860 and 1880, identifies remaining siblings in the household, and extends the chain of co-residence evidence before the 1880 census relationship column becomes available. Variant spellings Flynn, Flyn, Flinn, and Flyne should be checked.

Deeds, mortgages, and other land transactions involving Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County name witnesses and boundary-adjoining landowners — his FAN cluster. Boundary recitals in deeds explicitly identify the owners of adjoining parcels, who are frequently kin or close neighbors in immigrant communities of this era. A conveyance from Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn would be direct evidence of a father-son relationship. If Thomas transferred property near the end of his life, the deed or a subsequent administration transfer may name his heirs. Witnesses to deeds often appear repeatedly across transactions and can extend the FAN network. The Schuylkill County courthouse holds originals; FamilySearch may have digitized deed books for this period.

Patrick Flynn (born ca. 1845) would have been 16-20 years old during the Civil War (1861-1865). If he served in the Union Army, his compiled service record and pension file (Civil War Soldiers Index, collection 1910717, name-searchable) would contain extensive personal information: birthplace, age at enlistment, and — in a pension application — the names of parents or next of kin, siblings, and witnesses who could attest to his identity and family history. A pension deposition naming Thomas Flynn as his father would be independent corroborating evidence of parentage from a federal record, drawn from a context entirely separate from the census and death-certificate chain. Variant spellings should be checked.

Patrick was born in Ireland ca. 1845 and appears in Pennsylvania by the 1850 census, meaning the Flynn family immigrated ca. 1845-1850 during the Famine emigration. FamilySearch ship passenger manifests for this period are name-searchable. Famine-era manifests frequently list family groups traveling together, naming the head and accompanying family members with ages. A manifest listing Thomas Flynn with children of matching ages — including one consistent with Patrick — would be FAN evidence of the family unit from before the 1850 census, predating the Pennsylvania co-residence that forms the current chain of inference. Ports of Philadelphia, New York, and Boston all handled significant Irish Famine immigration. Variant spellings Flynn, Flyn, Flinn, and Flyne should be checked.

Other children of Thomas Flynn visible in the 1850 and 1860 census households would have death certificates — if they died after Pennsylvania's 1906 civil registration — naming Thomas Flynn as their father. These are independent FAN-corroborating sources: siblings' death certificates naming the same father strengthen the parentage case through separate informants who may have known Thomas Flynn personally or been present at Patrick's birth. The informants on siblings' death certificates (spouses, their own children) likely had firsthand knowledge of Thomas Flynn, making them stronger secondary sources than Patrick's son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at Patrick's birth. Date range set by the siblings' plausible lifespans: children born ca. 1840-1860 to Thomas Flynn (born ca. 1818) could realistically have died 1906-1950. Sibling names can be drawn from the 1850 and 1860 census household listings and from any christening records found in item 3.

**Surveyed facts already in the tree bearing on the question:**
- Silas Bankston (I1): birth ~1800, Feliciana Parish, Louisiana — unsourced birth fact
- Residence 1820, Feliciana Parish, Louisiana — sourced to the 1820 U.S. Federal Census (src_001, assertion a_001); no spouse, no parents, no children recorded

**Plan pl_001 — 6 items in execution order:**

- **pli_001** — marriage, East Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, 1824-1840, FamilySearch: "Louisiana, East Feliciana Parish Marriage Records, 1824-1900" is name-searchable (personCount 96,420). Co-equal primary with pli_002 — per loc_001 the 1824 Feliciana split was geographic, so both successors must be searched; try surname variants Bankson, Bankstone, Banxton.
- **pli_002** — marriage, West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, 1824-1840, FamilySearch: "Louisiana, West Feliciana Parish Marriage Records, 1824-1900" is name-searchable (personCount 79,760). Co-equal primary with pli_001 for the same reason; same variant spellings.
- **pli_003** — census, East and West Feliciana Parish, 1830, FamilySearch: name-searchable 1830 federal census; if Silas married circa 1828 the schedule should show him with a wife, and the enumeration district pins which parish he was in — corroborating date and directing the marriage-record search.
- **pli_004** — marriage (full-text), East and West Feliciana Parish, 1824-1840, FamilySearch: full-text co-occurrence search across image groups 003100201 (East, 88% indexed, full-text searchable) and 003100202 (West, 84% indexed, full-text searchable); catches transcription variants the name index misses. Route to search-full-text. Fallback for pli_002 (and pli_001 by the rationale).
- **pli_005** — marriage, East and West Feliciana Parish, 1824-1840, Ancestry: independently transcribed or indexed Feliciana marriage records that may supplement FamilySearch's coverage. Fallback for pli_004 (i.e., after all FamilySearch avenues are tried).
- **pli_006** — census (FAN), Feliciana Parish, 1820, FamilySearch: review the 1820 census image (src_001) for Silas's neighbors — persons adjacent on the enumeration page are potential marriage bondsmen or witnesses circa 1828; their names can then be cross-searched in the marriage registers to corroborate the parish and identify the record.

Total: 6 searches. No fallback relationship between pli_001 and pli_002 — both are mandatory co-equal searches given the unresolved geographic split. Fallback chain: pli_001/pli_002 → pli_004 (full-text) → pli_005 (Ancestry).

Hand-back: **search-records** for pli_001, pli_002, pli_003, and pli_006 (all FamilySearch); **search-full-text** for pli_004; **search-external-sites** for pli_005 (Ancestry).

---

This plan targets the question of where Silas Bankston married around 1828. Because Feliciana Parish divided into two separate parishes in 1824 — a geographic split, meaning his home could have ended up in either one — the plan searches both the East Feliciana and West Feliciana marriage registers on FamilySearch at the same time, not one as a backup for the other. If the standard name search misses him due to spelling variations like Bankson or Bankstone, a full-text search across the digitized volumes of both parishes acts as a safety net. The 1830 census is searched alongside the marriage registers because it would show Silas living with a wife, naming the parish and helping confirm which register to look in. A look at the neighbors listed next to Silas in the 1820 census may identify relatives or associates who witnessed or guaranteed the marriage, giving further clues about the location. If FamilySearch turns up nothing, Ancestry holds a separate set of Feliciana marriage records as a final fallback.

The next step is to run the two name searches in the East and West Feliciana Parish marriage registers on FamilySearch, alongside the 1830 census search and the 1820 census image review.

---

**Question:** Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?

**Key tree facts noted:**
- Michael Sheahan: residence 1870 Pennsylvania (county unknown), residence 1882 Schuylkill County, occupation "Miner" 1882 — all unsourced.
- Sibling Patrick Sheahan was already in Schuylkill County by 1875 (documented by a deed purchase), seven years before Michael's arrival.

**7-item research plan (pl_001), in execution order:**

| Item | Record Type | Place/Date | Repository | Purpose |
|------|-------------|------------|------------|---------|
| pli_001 | Census 1870 | Pennsylvania | FamilySearch | Where was Michael before Schuylkill? Locate Patrick too. |
| pli_002 | Census 1880 | Pennsylvania | FamilySearch | Last census before the ~1882 move; pin location and occupation. |
| pli_003 | Census 1900 | Schuylkill County | FamilySearch | Immigration year; did he come from Ireland or another US county? |
| pli_004 | Census 1910 | Schuylkill County | FamilySearch | Fallback for 1900; confirms mining career continuation. |
| pli_005 | Naturalization records | Schuylkill County, 1849–1915 | FamilySearch (browse) | Declaration of intent → arrival year, port, Irish county of origin. |
| pli_006 | Church records | Schuylkill County, 1842–1895 | FamilySearch | Irish Catholic parish acts to establish arrival date and family network. |
| pli_007 | Land/deed records | Schuylkill County, 1875–1900 | FamilySearch | Additional Sheahan deeds; FAN connections via witnesses and neighbors. |

**Recommended next step:** Run **pli_001** — search the 1870 U.S. Census on FamilySearch for Michael Sheahan (and variants Sheehan, Shea) in Pennsylvania.

response.objective: Determine why Michael Sheahan relocated to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882

openQuestions.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?

questionStatuses.nextStep: research-plan

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Michael's tree records a 1870 residence in 'Pennsylvania, United States' with no specific county. The United States Census, 1870 (name-searchable) would place him in a specific county, show his household composition, and establish his occupation twelve years before the Schuylkill County arrival. Crucially, the same search should locate Patrick Sheahan — who purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875 — to determine whether he preceded Michael to the coal region or whether both were still elsewhere in 1870. Finding Patrick already in Schuylkill County in 1870 would strengthen the chain-migration hypothesis as an explanation for Michael's move. Search variant spellings Sheehan, Shea.

The United States Census, 1880 (name-searchable) is the last federal census taken before Michael's documented Schuylkill County arrival around 1882. If he already appears in Schuylkill County in 1880, the 'circa 1882' date in the tree needs revision and points to a longer coal-region presence than recorded. If he appears elsewhere in Pennsylvania, the record would show his occupation just before the move — establishing whether mining was his trade before arriving or a new occupation he took up after. The 1880 schedule records each person's relationship to the head of household and occupation, both directly relevant to the migration question. Search variant spellings Sheehan, Shea.

The United States Census, 1900 (name-searchable) is the most informative post-arrival census for the migration question: for foreign-born persons it records the year of immigration to the United States and the number of years in the country, which would show whether Michael came directly from Ireland to Schuylkill County or spent years elsewhere in the US first. It also records marital status and years married, potentially revealing a marriage in the coal region after arrival. Eighteen years after the documented move, this census confirms long-term establishment.

The United States Census, 1910 (name-searchable) covers twenty-eight years after the move and complements the 1900 census: together the two bracket Michael's presence in the coal region across nearly three decades, establishing a sustained mining career rather than a transient one. The 1910 schedule also records immigration year for foreign-born persons. If the 1900 census does not yield a clear match, the 1910 census is the fallback for confirming his continued Schuylkill County residency and mining occupation.

The 'Sheahan' surname is Irish. If Michael was born in Ireland, he would have filed a declaration of intent ('first papers') with a local court. The Schuylkill County naturalization volume (image group 007936750, 1849–1915) is browse-only (personCount 0), meaning images must be browsed frame by frame. A declaration of intent would record his country of birth, port of arrival, arrival year, and sometimes his county of origin in Ireland — direct evidence for whether he came to the United States specifically for mining or arrived elsewhere first. A filing dated shortly after 1882 would corroborate arrival in the coal region at that time; an earlier filing in another county would show prior residence elsewhere. The locality guide notes some naturalization films for the anthracite region are browse-only, consistent with this volume's 0% record-searchable rate.

Two overlapping collections cover Schuylkill County church records: the Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable, and an image-group volume (007936751, 1842–1895, partly in German) is browse-only (personCount 0). The locality guide notes that Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875), with registers held at the parish and diocesan level, not the county. The Irish Catholic community in the anthracite coal region used the local parish as the primary social institution for chain migration: a letter of transfer, a marriage or baptism dated shortly after 1882, or a godparent listed as Patrick Sheahan would establish Michael's arrival date and show the family network that drew him to Schuylkill County. Search also under the variant spelling Sheehan. Start with the name-searchable collection; if no match, browse the image group.

Patrick Sheahan (sibling of Michael, person I2) is documented purchasing land in Schuylkill County in 1875, seven years before Michael's arrival (Deed Book 42, p. 118, already in the tree). The Schuylkill County deed records volume (image group 007936752, 1815–1900, 22% record-searchable) may contain additional Sheahan transactions — Michael appearing as buyer, grantor, or witness in deeds near Patrick's 1875 purchase — which would show the family's economic network and whether property acquisition alongside Patrick was a pull factor for Michael's move. The locality guide notes that much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers, so a direct purchase by Michael would be economically notable. Deed witnesses and adjoining landowners are a FAN source: they frequently were kin or close associates who can corroborate the chain-migration pattern.

**Mode:** Create (first plan) — question q_001: "Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?"

**Tree facts found before planning:**
- Michael Sheahan (I1): Residence 1870, "Pennsylvania, United States" — no specific county, no source.
- Michael Sheahan (I1): Residence 1882, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — no source.
- Michael Sheahan (I1): Occupation "Miner," 1882 — no source.
- Patrick Sheahan (I2, sibling): Residence 1875, Schuylkill County — sourced to Deed Book 42, p. 118 (land purchase). Patrick was in the coal region seven years before Michael.
- Parent (I3): surname Sheahan only; no given name, dates, gender or location recorded.

**Plan pl_001 — 7 items in execution order:**

- `pli_001` — census, Pennsylvania United States, 1870, FamilySearch. The 1870 census (name-searchable) places Michael in a specific county and shows his occupation twelve years before Schuylkill; also locates Patrick in the same search to test whether Patrick preceded him to the coal region.
- `pli_002` — census, Pennsylvania United States, 1880, FamilySearch. The 1880 census (name-searchable) is the last federal census before the circa-1882 move; if Michael already appears in Schuylkill County, the date needs revision; if elsewhere, shows his occupation and location just before moving.
- `pli_003` — census, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1900, FamilySearch. The 1900 census (name-searchable) records immigration year and years in the US for foreign-born persons — directly shows whether Michael came to Schuylkill County from Ireland or from another US location first.
- `pli_004` — census, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1910, FamilySearch. Fallback for pli_003; confirms sustained mining career twenty-eight years after the move; also records immigration year for foreign-born.
- `pli_005` — immigration (naturalization), Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1849–1915, FamilySearch. Browse-only (personCount 0) — image group 007936750; a declaration of intent would record arrival year, port, and Irish county of origin, directly addressing whether Michael came to the US for mining or settled first elsewhere.
- `pli_006` — church, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1842–1895, FamilySearch. The name-searchable Schuylkill County Church Records collection (then browse-only image group 007936751 as fallback); an Irish Catholic parish act shortly after 1882 or a godparent of "Patrick Sheahan" establishes arrival date and the family network behind the move.
- `pli_007` — land, Schuylkill County Pennsylvania, 1875–1900, FamilySearch. Deed volume 007936752 (22% record-searchable); searches for additional Sheahan deed transactions beyond Patrick's 1875 purchase, including Michael as buyer or witness, and FAN connections via deed witnesses and adjoining landowners.

No baptism-may-not-exist item is warranted: this is a migration motivation question, not a parentage or birth question.

**Execution:** Every item is a FamilySearch source. The delegation does not authorize immediate execution, so the recommended next step is to hand pli_001 to search-records.

This plan is for the question of why Michael Sheahan relocated to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882, with family tradition pointing to anthracite coal-mining work. The plan works in order through the federal census years — 1870, 1880, 1900, and 1910 — to track where Michael was before, just before, and long after the move, and what occupation he held at each point. Then it turns to the Schuylkill County naturalization records (browsed image by image, since they are not name-indexed) to find any declaration of intent that would record when he arrived in the United States and from where in Ireland. The church records come next, because Irish Catholic parishes in the anthracite coal region were the social infrastructure for chain migration, and an act dated soon after 1882 — or one with his sibling Patrick as godparent — would pin down the arrival date and the family connection that drew him. Finally, the deed records are searched for additional Sheahan land transactions beyond Patrick's 1875 purchase, which would show whether property acquisition alongside his brother was part of the economic pull.

The next step is to run the first search: the 1870 United States Census on FamilySearch, looking for Michael Sheahan (and variants Sheehan, Shea) in Pennsylvania.

The United States Census, 1870 (name-searchable) would place him in a specific county, show his household composition, and establish his occupation twelve years before the Schuylkill County arrival. Crucially, the same search should locate Patrick Sheahan — who purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875 — to determine whether he preceded Michael to the coal region or whether both were still elsewhere in 1870. Finding Patrick already in Schuylkill County in 1870 would strengthen the chain-migration hypothesis as an explanation for Michael's move. Search variant spellings Sheehan, Shea.

The United States Census, 1880 (name-searchable) is the last federal census taken before Michael's documented Schuylkill County arrival around 1882. If he already appears in Schuylkill County in 1880, the 'circa 1882' date in the tree needs revision and points to a longer coal-region presence than recorded. If he appears elsewhere in Pennsylvania, the record would show his occupation just before the move — establishing whether mining was his trade before arriving or a new occupation he took up after. The 1880 schedule records each person's relationship to the head of household and occupation, both directly relevant to the migration question. Search variant spellings Sheehan, Shea.

The United States Census, 1900 (name-searchable) is the most informative post-arrival census for the migration question: for foreign-born persons it records the year of immigration to the United States and the number of years in the country, which would show whether Michael came directly from Ireland to Schuylkill County or spent years elsewhere in the US first. It also records marital status and years married, potentially revealing a marriage in the coal region after arrival. Eighteen years after the documented move, this census confirms long-term establishment.

The United States Census, 1910 (name-searchable) covers twenty-eight years after the move and complements the 1900 census: together the two bracket Michael's presence in the coal region across nearly three decades, establishing a sustained mining career rather than a transient one. The 1910 schedule also records immigration year for foreign-born persons. If the 1900 census does not yield a clear match, the 1910 census is the fallback for confirming his continued Schuylkill County residency and mining occupation.

The 'Sheahan' surname is Irish. If Michael was born in Ireland, he would have filed a declaration of intent ('first papers') with a local court. The Schuylkill County naturalization volume (image group 007936750, 1849–1915) is browse-only (personCount 0), meaning images must be browsed frame by frame. A declaration of intent would record his country of birth, port of arrival, arrival year, and sometimes his county of origin in Ireland — direct evidence for whether he came to the United States specifically for mining or arrived elsewhere first. A filing dated shortly after 1882 would corroborate arrival in the coal region at that time; an earlier filing in another county would show prior residence elsewhere. The locality guide notes some naturalization films for the anthracite region are browse-only, consistent with this volume's 0% record-searchable rate.

Two overlapping collections cover Schuylkill County church records: the Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable, and an image-group volume (007936751, 1842–1895, partly in German) is browse-only (personCount 0). The locality guide notes that Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875), with registers held at the parish and diocesan level, not the county. The Irish Catholic community in the anthracite coal region used the local parish as the primary social institution for chain migration: a letter of transfer, a marriage or baptism dated shortly after 1882, or a godparent listed as Patrick Sheahan would establish Michael's arrival date and show the family network that drew him to Schuylkill County. Search also under the variant spelling Sheehan. Start with the name-searchable collection; if no match, browse the image group.

Patrick Sheahan (sibling of Michael, person I2) is documented purchasing land in Schuylkill County in 1875, seven years before Michael's arrival (Deed Book 42, p. 118, already in the tree). The Schuylkill County deed records volume (image group 007936752, 1815–1900, 22% record-searchable) may contain additional Sheahan transactions — Michael appearing as buyer, grantor, or witness in deeds near Patrick's 1875 purchase — which would show the family's economic network and whether property acquisition alongside Patrick was a pull factor for Michael's move. The locality guide notes that much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers, so a direct purchase by Michael would be economically notable. Deed witnesses and adjoining landowners are a FAN source: they frequently were kin or close associates who can corroborate the chain-migration pattern.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

Searching all of Pennsylvania for Michael Sheahan — also try Sheehan and Shehane — will show his exact county and occupation at the time, establishing the baseline before the move. The same search should locate Patrick Sheahan in Schuylkill County; the deed record (S2, primary) places Patrick there as early as 1875, and confirming him in 1880 documents that a family member had already established himself in the county, supporting a chain migration reading of Michael's later arrival. Patrick's occupation field may also show whether the family already had a foothold in mining work.

The 1870 US Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) covers the earliest year the tree documents: S1 (compiled) places Michael in 'Pennsylvania, United States' in 1870 without specifying which county. This search will identify which county he was in twelve years before the move, his occupation at that time, and whether the household points to an origin community or family group. Search Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehane. Finding him in a non-mining occupation or in a county distant from the anthracite coal region strengthens the inference that the 1882 move was driven by the availability of mining work specifically in Schuylkill County.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, covering 1708-1985) holds Roman Catholic sacramental registers, the most likely denomination for an Irish immigrant named Sheahan. Baptism, marriage, and burial entries routinely record the subject's occupation and residence, which could independently verify that Michael was working as a miner after 1882, corroborating the compiled entry in S1. The locality guide (loc_001) notes that pre-1906 vital events are documented in church rather than civil registers, and that Schuylkill County parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia. Search Sheahan and Sheehan.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) would show Michael's residence and occupation eighteen years after the move. Confirming him still in Schuylkill County and still recorded as a miner would corroborate S1's 1882 occupation entry (compiled) and demonstrate that mining was a sustained livelihood, not a temporary circumstance. Critically, the 1900 schedule records each person's birth country and the number of years they had been in the United States — information that could narrow Michael's national origin and the timing of his immigration, both relevant to understanding the migration context.

Schuylkill County naturalization records (image group 007936750, browse-only (personCount 0), covering 1849-1915) are the only Schuylkill County source that would state when Michael arrived in the United States and — crucially — where in the US he lived before declaring intent or filing his final petition. A declaration of intent or final petition often names the county of prior residence and a witness; given Patrick's documented presence in Schuylkill County from 1875 (S2), Patrick may appear as a witness, directly linking the two brothers. Browse the volume for Sheahan and Sheehan entries between 1875 and 1905.

Pennsylvania's state mine inspectors filed annual reports organized by mining district, naming each colliery in the district and sometimes recording individual accidents, fatalities, and workforce details. The anthracite coal region around Schuylkill County constituted a designated inspection district. These reports are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg and are the most direct occupation-specific evidence available for the question: they substantiate that anthracite mining was the dominant employer in the area where Michael settled. In accident or fatality entries, individual miners are named, which could confirm Michael's presence at a specific colliery. Even where Michael cannot be identified by name, the reports contextualize the scale of the mining industry that would have drawn a laborer to the county in 1882.

agent_returns.text:
Mode: **create** — first plan for q_001, "Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?"

**Tree facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- Michael Sheahan: Residence "Pennsylvania, United States" in 1870 — compiled source S1, county unspecified, needs original-record verification
- Michael Sheahan: Residence Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania in 1882 — compiled source S1
- Michael Sheahan: Occupation "Miner" in 1882 — compiled source S1, needs original-record verification
- Patrick Sheahan (sibling): Residence Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania in 1875 — primary deed record S2; Patrick preceded Michael to Schuylkill County by roughly seven years, the strongest lead for a chain migration explanation

**Plan pl_001 — 6 items in execution order:**

- **pli_001** | census | Pennsylvania, United States | 1880 | FamilySearch | name-searchable (collection 1417683); the closest pre-move record, showing Michael's county and occupation two years before the move; same search locates Patrick in Schuylkill County to document his 1880 presence (S2 places him there in 1875) and his mining occupation, supporting chain migration
- **pli_002** | census | Pennsylvania, United States | 1870 | FamilySearch | name-searchable (collection 1438024); the earliest tree-documented year (S1 gives only "Pennsylvania"), will identify which county Michael was in twelve years before the move and whether his occupation was then unrelated to mining; search Sheahan / Sheehan / Shehane
- **pli_003** | church | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania | 1882–1910 | FamilySearch | name-searchable (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH); Roman Catholic parish sacramental registers record occupation and residence, independently verifying the S1 "Miner" entry for Michael post-1882; pre-1906 vital events appear here rather than in civil registers (loc_001)
- **pli_004** | census | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania | 1900 | FamilySearch | name-searchable (collection 1325221); confirms Michael's continued residence and sustained mining occupation eighteen years post-move; 1900 schedule also records birth country and years in the US, narrowing immigration origin and timing
- **pli_005** | immigration | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania | 1875–1905 | FamilySearch | browse-only (personCount 0), image group 007936750, naturalization records 1849–1915; a declaration of intent or final petition states the county of prior US residence and names a witness — Patrick may appear as witness, directly linking both brothers; browse for Sheahan / Sheehan entries
- **pli_006** | other | Schuylkill, Pennsylvania | 1882–1900 | Pennsylvania State Archives | Pennsylvania mine inspector annual reports, filed by district, name each operating colliery; individual accident and fatality entries can name miners; the most direct occupation-specific evidence for the "mining work" hypothesis; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg

**Breadth self-check passed:** census (federal, multiple years), church, immigration/naturalization, occupation-specific government records — four distinct record types; two repositories (FamilySearch and Pennsylvania State Archives); variant spellings noted in each rationale; two jurisdictions (all-Pennsylvania pre-move, Schuylkill County post-move); date range 1870–1910 spanning the question's full window.

Hand-back: this is a migration question with six items — pli_001 through pli_004 go to **search-records** (FamilySearch collections), pli_005 also to **search-records** (browse of the FamilySearch naturalization image group), and pli_006 to **search-external-sites** (Pennsylvania State Archives). The delegation did not authorize execution, so no items are passed forward here.

---

This plan addresses the question of why Michael Sheahan relocated to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882. It begins with the 1880 federal census, the closest snapshot before his move, to pin down exactly where in Pennsylvania he was living and what work he was doing at the time — and to confirm that his brother Patrick was already established in Schuylkill County, since a deed from 1875 already shows Patrick there seven years before Michael arrived. The 1870 census goes further back to show whether Michael had any connection to mining at all before the move. From there the plan shifts to post-1882 records: Catholic parish registers in Schuylkill County, which recorded occupations and would independently confirm the mining claim; the 1900 federal census, which also captures how many years each person had been in the United States; browse-only naturalization records filed in the county court, which can state where in the US a person lived before declaring intent and who witnessed the filing; and the Pennsylvania state mine inspector annual reports, the most direct evidence that Michael was working at a specific anthracite colliery.

When searching begins, the FamilySearch items — the two federal censuses, the church records, the 1900 census, and the naturalization image browse — will be searched first since they are free and online, and the Pennsylvania State Archives item will follow.

items.rationale: The 1880 US Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) is the closest pre-move record: taken in June 1880, roughly two years before Michael's documented 1882 arrival in Schuylkill County (S1, compiled). Searching all of Pennsylvania for Michael Sheahan — also try Sheehan and Shehane — will show his exact county and occupation at the time, establishing the baseline before the move. The same search should locate Patrick Sheahan in Schuylkill County; the deed record (S2, primary) places Patrick there as early as 1875, and confirming him in 1880 documents that a family member had already established himself in the county, supporting a chain migration reading of Michael's later arrival. Patrick's occupation field may also show whether the family already had a foothold in mining work.

The 1870 US Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) covers the earliest year the tree documents: S1 (compiled) places Michael in 'Pennsylvania, United States' in 1870 without specifying which county. This search will identify which county he was in twelve years before the move, his occupation at that time, and whether the household points to an origin community or family group. Search Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehane. Finding him in a non-mining occupation or in a county distant from the anthracite coal region strengthens the inference that the 1882 move was driven by the availability of mining work specifically in Schuylkill County.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, covering 1708-1985) holds Roman Catholic sacramental registers, the most likely denomination for an Irish immigrant named Sheahan. Baptism, marriage, and burial entries routinely record the subject's occupation and residence, which could independently verify that Michael was working as a miner after 1882, corroborating the compiled entry in S1. The locality guide (loc_001) notes that pre-1906 vital events are documented in church rather than civil registers, and that Schuylkill County parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia. Search Sheahan and Sheehan.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) would show Michael's residence and occupation eighteen years after the move. Confirming him still in Schuylkill County and still recorded as a miner would corroborate S1's 1882 occupation entry (compiled) and demonstrate that mining was a sustained livelihood, not a temporary circumstance. Critically, the 1900 schedule records each person's birth country and the number of years they had been in the United States — information that could narrow Michael's national origin and the timing of his immigration, both relevant to understanding the migration context.

Schuylkill County naturalization records (image group 007936750, browse-only (personCount 0), covering 1849-1915) are the only Schuylkill County source that would state when Michael arrived in the United States and — crucially — where in the US he lived before declaring intent or filing his final petition. A declaration of intent or final petition often names the county of prior residence and a witness; given Patrick's documented presence in Schuylkill County from 1875 (S2), Patrick may appear as a witness, directly linking the two brothers. Browse the volume for Sheahan and Sheehan entries between 1875 and 1905.

Pennsylvania's state mine inspectors filed annual reports organized by mining district, naming each colliery in the district and sometimes recording individual accidents, fatalities, and workforce details. The anthracite coal region around Schuylkill County constituted a designated inspection district. These reports are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg and are the most direct occupation-specific evidence available for the question: they substantiate that anthracite mining was the dominant employer in the area where Michael settled. In accident or fatality entries, individual miners are named, which could confirm Michael's presence at a specific colliery. Even where Michael cannot be identified by name, the reports contextualize the scale of the mining industry that would have drawn a laborer to the county in 1882.
