quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: The 1880 census (United States Census, 1880; collection 1417683; name-searchable) falls two years before Michael's reported arrival in Schuylkill County per tree fact F2. If he appears in Schuylkill County in 1880, the move predates family tradition — a key factual correction. If found elsewhere in Pennsylvania, it anchors his last known location before migration. The Occupation column directly records each person's work, providing independent evidence of mining employment. Search under 'Sheahan' and variants including 'Sheehan' and 'Shahan,' which enumerators commonly substituted.

The tree records an unsourced 1870 Pennsylvania residence (fact F1, place given only as 'Pennsylvania, United States'). The 1870 census (United States Census, 1870; collection 1438024; name-searchable) would document which county in Pennsylvania Michael was in before any move to Schuylkill County, confirming that unsourced fact and supplying the precise departure point for the migration. The Occupation column also records work, establishing whether he was already a miner in 1870 or took up that occupation after arriving in Schuylkill County. Search under 'Sheahan,' 'Sheehan,' and 'Shahan.'

The 1900 census (United States Census, 1900; collection 1325221; name-searchable) would confirm Michael's continued settlement in Schuylkill County after 1882 and document his occupation, household composition, and — uniquely in this schedule — the number of years he had lived in the United States, directly bearing on whether his reported 1882 arrival in Schuylkill County coincided with his US arrival. If the 1880 census finds him in Schuylkill County already, the 1900 record corroborates the settlement pattern and occupation over time.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH; name-searchable; date range 1708–1985) covers sacramental registers from Roman Catholic and other denominations. Sheahan is an Irish surname closely associated with Catholic practice. loc_001 notes that Pennsylvania statewide civil registration did not begin until 1906, making church records the primary source for events before that date in this county. Catholic parishes in the Schuylkill anthracite region were often organized by national origin (Irish, Welsh, Polish), so a parish affiliation would corroborate both his presence in the county and the Irish chain-migration context that family tradition implies. Search under 'Sheahan,' 'Sheehan,' and 'Shahan.'

Image group 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849–1915; browse-only (personCount 0)) records declarations of intent and final petitions filed in the county court. Naturalization papers state the declarant's country of birth, port of entry, and approximate date of US arrival — directly establishing whether Michael was Irish-born and when he came to the United States. loc_001 flags that some naturalization films for the anthracite region are browse-only image groups. Browse image-by-image through this volume for entries under 'Sheahan,' 'Sheehan,' and 'Shahan.'

The Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines published annual inspection reports from 1870 onward; these reports named the mines in each inspection district, their operators, and in some years the names of employees and accident victims. Mine operator employment ledgers and payroll books for the Schuylkill anthracite region are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and, for Reading Company records, at the Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, DE). These records are not in any FamilySearch collection. Access requires contacting the repository directly. This item targets the most direct possible evidence that Michael worked in anthracite mining — establishing occupation as a documented employment record rather than a census label, and potentially naming the specific mine or company he worked for.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.

The 1880 census introduced the relationship-to-head column for the first time. Patrick (approximately 35 in 1880) is likely heading his own household by this date. Even separate entries for Patrick and Thomas without a shared household would confirm continued Pennsylvania residence and age consistency. The 1890 census is excluded — approximately 80% was destroyed in a 1921 fire at the Commerce Department building and is not available for Pennsylvania. The collection 'United States Census, 1880' is name-searchable. Include Flynn / Flinn / Flin variants.

Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) would be approximately 55 in 1900, eight years before his death in March 1908. The 1900 census records each person's birth month and year and each person's parents' country of birth — both items directly relevant to the proof. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) would be approximately 82 if still living; an elderly parent often moved into an adult child's household, and if Thomas appears alongside Patrick, the relationship column would supply direct parentage evidence. **Step 1 survey — facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- I1 Patrick Flynn: Birth ~1845, Ireland (sourced from 1850 census); Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (sourced from death certificate). No post-1860 facts in the tree.
- I2 Thomas Flynn: Birth ~1818, Ireland. No death date or any post-1860 fact recorded.
- The R1 ParentChild relationship (Thomas → Patrick) is already in the tree, sourced from the 1850 census, 1860 census, and death certificate — but rated only "probable / gap" in ps_001 because the census records before 1880 do not state relationships and the death certificate informant is secondary.
- The proof summary explicitly identifies 1870, 1880, 1900 censuses and Thomas's probate as the remaining gaps.

**Plan pl_003 — four items in execution order:**

- **pli_006** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | 1870 | FamilySearch | no fallback — Patrick (~25) may still share Thomas's (~52) household; the 1870 census does not state relationships but co-residence would sustain the household link; search both men by name with Flynn/Flinn/Flin variants; broaden to adjacent counties if neither is found in Schuylkill. Collection "United States Census, 1870" is name-searchable.

- **pli_007** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | 1880 | FamilySearch | no fallback — the 1880 census introduced the relationship-to-head column; if Thomas (~62) appears in Patrick's (~35) household listed as "father," that is the first direct census evidence of parentage and would advance the conclusion to proved. The 1890 census is excluded (~80% destroyed in the 1921 Commerce Dept. fire). Collection "United States Census, 1880" is name-searchable.

- **pli_008** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | 1900 | FamilySearch | no fallback — Patrick (~55) is eight years from his 1908 death; the 1900 census records birth month/year and parents' country of birth; Thomas (~82 if living) may now be in Patrick's household as an elderly dependent, supplying the relationship column entry that would clinch the conclusion. Collection "United States Census, 1900" is name-searchable.

- **pli_009** | probate | Schuylkill County, PA | 1860–1900 | FamilySearch — the date window is bounded by Thomas's plausible lifespan (~1818 birth; last seen 1860); a will naming Patrick as a son is the strongest available parentage evidence; Schuylkill County Register of Wills holds records from 1811 (locality survey loc_001). If the FamilySearch index returns nothing, browse the county docket images for the same range. Explicitly named as a gap in ps_001.

**Hand-back:** Search-records for all four items (all FamilySearch). The delegation did not authorize execution, so I am not handing back as already authorized.

---

The research plan is for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were — a conclusion currently supported but not proved because the census records from before 1880 don't state family relationships and the only person who named Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father on a document was a son-in-law reporting decades after the fact. The plan opens four searches in order: the 1870 federal census to track where Patrick and Thomas Flynn were living when Patrick was about 25; the 1880 federal census, which for the first time asked each person's relationship to the head of household (making it the census most likely to produce a direct "father" entry if the two men shared a roof); the 1900 federal census, which would show Patrick in his mid-fifties and might show an elderly Thomas living with him, again with the relationship column; and finally the Schuylkill County probate records from roughly 1860 to 1900, covering the span when Thomas most likely died — a will naming Patrick as a son would be the single strongest piece of evidence available. The 1890 census is not included because about 80 percent of it was destroyed in a fire in 1921 and Pennsylvania records largely did not survive. All four searches run on FamilySearch, where the census collections and Pennsylvania probate records are fully name-searchable.

Next, a search of those four collections on FamilySearch will be run, starting with the 1870 census and working forward.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

This item also satisfies the requirement for the subject's own death or burial entry when a baptism is inaccessible: Patrick was born in Ireland ~1845, so no Schuylkill County baptism record can be expected. Variant spellings Flynn / Flinn should be checked if the first search returns nothing.

S2 (1860 U.S. Federal Census, Schuylkill Co., dwelling 112) is already cited on the R1 parent-child relationship in the tree but no assertions for q_001 have been extracted from it. The United States Census 1860 collection (1473181) is name-searchable. A household showing Thomas and Patrick ten years on — with Thomas's wife named for the first time — would corroborate the family unit and may supply the mother's name. The timeline's medium gap for 1851–1860 also flags this year as unworked. Variant spellings Flynn / Flinn should be tried.

A will or administration naming Patrick as Thomas Flynn's heir is the most direct parentage evidence available from county records. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is listed among the tree's source descriptions but has not been attached to any person or relationship, and no assertions have been extracted. The Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 collection (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), so this requires image-by-image browsing; the Schuylkill County probate image group 007936749 (1851-1930, 0% record-searchable) is the specific volume. Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton Counties, and its Register of Wills records run from that founding. The locality guide confirms probate records are held by the county Register of Wills. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) could plausibly have died ca. 1860–1890; Thomas's estimated lifespan sets this date window, not Patrick's own research period.

The couple's marriage record: (a) confirms Thomas and his wife as a unit; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which census records do not state; (c) corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father by its date relative to Patrick's birth ~1845. If the name-searchable collection does not cover the relevant parish, the browse-only church records image group 007936751 (1842-1895, personCount 0) is the fallback. Note: this marriage record confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple but does not by itself prove Patrick is their child — a record placing Patrick with them is still required. The 1870 U.S. Federal Census collection (1438024) is name-searchable. By 1870 Patrick (~25) would likely be heading his own household or still living with Thomas (~52 if alive). A record showing Patrick adjacent to or in Thomas's household, or a consistent wife appearing alongside Thomas across 1860 and 1870, strengthens the family identification. An external-collection copy (ancestry:7163) is available on Ancestry if the FamilySearch search is inconclusive. Variant spellings Flynn / Flinn should be tried.

Patrick (~35) in 1880 and Thomas (~62 if alive) may appear; an explicit 'son' or 'father' relationship label is stronger evidence than the inferred household position on which the 1850 and 1860 extractions rest. If Thomas is already dead by 1880, Patrick's own household entry may still name his birthplace as Ireland and his parents' birthplaces.

This is the required FAN item for this parentage question. Thomas Flynn was born in Ireland ~1818 and almost certainly went through naturalization in Pennsylvania before 1870. Naturalization declarations and petitions (first and second papers) frequently name the applicant's wife, children, and witnesses — who were often neighbors, kin, or associates in the Irish immigrant anthracite-coal communities. The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records image group 007936750 (1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0), requiring image-by-image review per the locality guide's quirks note on browse-only films for the coal region. Witnesses who appear alongside Thomas are a FAN-cluster lead that may name Patrick directly or identify relatives who held further records.

The 1900 U.S. Federal Census collection (1325221) is name-searchable. Patrick (~55 in 1900) should appear in Schuylkill County; the 1900 schedule records each person's parents' birthplace (country) and years married. If Patrick's entry states his mother's and father's birthplace as Ireland it corroborates the Irish Flynn family origin. Any siblings still in the county under the Flynn surname would also be visible nearby, providing additional FAN-cluster leads. Thomas is likely deceased by 1900 (born ~1818), but this census closes the window before Patrick's 1908 death.

Plan `pl_002` written with 8 items (`pli_004`–`pli_011`). Here is the full return.

- I1 Patrick Flynn: death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (sourced to S3, death cert no. 4521). No q_001 assertions extracted from S3.
- I2 Thomas Flynn: birth ~1818, Ireland — no source attached to this person record.
- Relationship R1 (Thomas → Patrick): cited to S1 (1850 census), S2 (1860 census, Schuylkill Co., dwelling 112), and S3 (death cert), all at quality 2 (inferred/secondary). No assertions for q_001 have been extracted from S2 or S3.
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) listed as a tree source description but not attached to any person or relationship; no assertions extracted.
- No FamilySearch person ID (ark) recorded for Patrick (I1) — the fs_hints review item was omitted because the router cannot execute it without a PID.

**Plan `pl_002` — 8 items in execution order:**

- `pli_004` — vital_record, Pennsylvania, 1908, FamilySearch. Death cert S3 (cert no. 4521) is already in the tree but its parent-name fields have not been extracted as assertions for q_001. Pennsylvania civil registration began in 1906; the informant was required to name the parents. This is the highest-probability immediate step and also serves as the subject's own end-of-life record standing in for an inaccessible Irish baptism.

- `pli_005` — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1860, FamilySearch (collection 1473181, name-searchable). S2 (1860 census, dwelling 112) is already cited on the tree relationship but no q_001 assertions were extracted. This record may name Thomas's wife for the first time and shows the household 10 years on from 1850.

- `pli_006` — probate, Schuylkill County PA, 1860-1890, FamilySearch (collection 1999196, browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749). S4 is listed in the tree but unattached. A will or administration naming Patrick as heir is direct parentage evidence. Date window set by Thomas's estimated lifespan (~1818 birth), not Patrick's period.

- `pli_007` — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1840-1865, FamilySearch (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable). Dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage: supplies the mother's maiden name, confirms the couple as a unit, and corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father by date. Does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Browse-only image group 007936751 is the fallback if the name-searchable collection misses the parish.

- `pli_008` — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, FamilySearch (collection 1438024, name-searchable). Patrick (~25) and Thomas (~52 if alive). Ancestry external copy (ancestry:7163) is a fallback if FamilySearch is inconclusive.

- `pli_009` — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, FamilySearch (collection 1417683, name-searchable). First census to record explicit relationship-to-head labels; an explicit "son" or "father" entry is stronger than inferred household position.

- `pli_010` — court (naturalization), Schuylkill County PA, 1849-1880, FamilySearch (image group 007936750, browse-only (personCount 0)). Required FAN item. Thomas's naturalization papers frequently named his wife, children, and witnesses — neighbors and kin in the Irish anthracite-coal community who are direct leads to Patrick's family network.

- `pli_011` — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1900, FamilySearch (collection 1325221, name-searchable). Patrick (~55); 1900 schedule records parents' birthplace by country and years married. Closes the window before the 1908 death; any Flynn siblings still nearby are additional FAN leads.

**Death/burial item for baptism self-check:** `pli_004` (Patrick's 1908 death certificate) satisfies this — his birth ~1845 in Ireland places the baptism entirely outside Schuylkill County records.

**Total scope:** 8 searches. All repositories are FamilySearch; three items require image browsing (probate, church-browse fallback, naturalization).

**Hand-back:** All 8 items target FamilySearch — execution goes to search-records. The delegation did not authorize immediate execution, so: would you like me to start executing this plan?

The question for this plan is identifying the parents of Patrick Flynn, an Irish-born immigrant who died in 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. The plan opens with the two records already sitting in the family tree but never formally examined for this question: Patrick's 1908 death certificate (which Pennsylvania required to name the parents) and the 1860 census entry for Thomas Flynn's household. From there it searches the county Register of Wills for Thomas's probate file — a will naming Patrick as heir would be the most direct proof of parentage — and then the Schuylkill County church records for Thomas's marriage, which would name Patrick's mother for the first time. Four successive census years (1870, 1880, 1900, and the 1860 one already in hand) track the household across Patrick's adult life, with the 1880 entry especially valuable because that census was the first to label each person's relationship to the head of household. Finally, Thomas Flynn's naturalization papers are searched as the required family-and-associates item, since Irish immigrants in the coal region routinely named wives, children, and neighbors as witnesses, which can point directly to Patrick or to relatives holding further records.

The next step is to extract the parent-name fields from Patrick's 1908 death certificate, then work through the remaining seven searches in the order listed.

Per loc_002, the Smith County marriage volumes for 1857-1876 are name-searchable and full-text searchable. Volume 005154190 (1860 U.S. Census, Blount County, Alabama) is name-searchable (99% indexed). Search for a Wood household with a head born roughly 1820-1840 and a very young daughter. Examine the immediate neighbors of any Wood household for the FAN cluster — antebellum neighbors were frequently kin, and an adjacent household sharing the surname or with cross-family naming patterns can corroborate the parentage connection.

Martha's stated birth place is Georgia (approximately 1859, tree fact F3, no source cited). If her family had not yet migrated out of Georgia by June 1860, they would appear in the Georgia federal census. The 1860 United States Census (collection 1927240) is name-searchable and covers all Georgia counties. This is a co-equal primary alongside the Alabama 1860 search (pli_002) — not a fallback — because the family's location at census time is unknown and both states must be searched.

Martha was born approximately 1859 and would not appear in the 1850 census, but her parents would — likely as a young married couple, possibly with older siblings whose identities could confirm the family. Searching the 1850 federal census for a Wood family in Georgia, the stated birth state, would establish the parents' given names and origins a decade before Martha was born. The 1850 census is available name-searchable on FamilySearch. If the 1860 Alabama search (pli_002) identifies the candidate Wood household, extend this search to Alabama as well to trace the family's prior location.

A dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other is required for this parentage question. If Martha's parents are the Wood family identified in Blount County, Alabama (pli_002), their marriage record would confirm the couple as a unit and supply the mother's maiden name — which census records and death certificates usually omit. Volume 007316662 (Blount County, Alabama Marriage Records, 1820-1888) is name-searchable (92% indexed) and full-text searchable. Date range is 1820-1858, bounded by the father's plausible lifespan: a father born approximately 1820-1840 who had a child in 1859 would have married before Martha's birth. Note: this couple's marriage proves they wed and dates their union but is not by itself evidence that Martha is their child — that link requires a record placing her with the parents.

If Martha's parents married in Georgia before migrating to Alabama or Texas, their marriage would appear here rather than in Alabama. Georgia, County Marriages, 1785-1950 (collection 1420203) is name-searchable. Search for a Wood groom marrying approximately 1840-1858. Martha J (I2) has no recorded death date or place in the project tree. Date range 1855-1920 is bounded by the father's plausible lifespan: a father who had a child in 1859 was probably born approximately 1820-1840 and could have died any time from the late 1850s to approximately 1920. Fallback if the Georgia probate search (pli_008) yields nothing: if the Wood family settled in Blount County, Alabama, the father's estate would be filed there. output.text_response:
**Mode:** Add-new — prior plan `pl_002` was already `completed`; proof summary `ps_001` is at `probable`, not `proved`.

**Question:** q_001 — "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Step 1 survey — facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): birth ~1845 Ireland, sourced to the 1850 census; death 12 March 1908 Schuylkill County PA, sourced to death certificate no. 4521
- Thomas Flynn (I2): birth ~1818 Ireland; no sources attached to the individual; no wife recorded anywhere in the tree
- 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage): Patrick in Thomas Flynn household — indirect parentage evidence (household position and shared surname)
- 1860 census (FamilySearch): Patrick age 15 still in Thomas Flynn household — continues indirect pattern
- 1908 death certificate: names Thomas Flynn as father; informant is son-in-law James Brown (secondary)
- Proof summary `ps_001` rated "probable"; stated gaps: 1870, 1880, 1900 censuses and Thomas Flynn's probate not yet searched
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) present in source list; zero assertions extracted from it

---

**Plan: pl_003 — 7 items**

- **`pli_006`** — census, Schuylkill County PA, FamilySearch, **1880**: the first census with an explicit relationship column (collection 1417683, name-searchable); if Patrick appears with Thomas, the enumerated relationship is direct parentage evidence; may also introduce Thomas's wife
- **`pli_007`** — census, Schuylkill County PA, FamilySearch, **1870**: extends the co-residence pattern across a third decade (collection 1438024, name-searchable); 1870 may also introduce Thomas's wife by name for the first time
- **`pli_008`** — census, Schuylkill County PA, FamilySearch, **1900**: Patrick (~55) died in 1908 and must be in the 1900 enumeration; records years in US and naturalization status; secondary aim is finding Thomas if he survived to ~82
- **`pli_009`** — probate, Schuylkill County PA, FamilySearch, **1860–1910**: image group 007936749 covering 1851–1930; date range set by Thomas's plausible death window (born ~1818, last seen 1860); a will naming Patrick as son is direct parentage evidence; S4 already in source list but uncited
- **`pli_010`** — church, Schuylkill County PA, FamilySearch, **1845–1910**: name-searchable (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH); required FAN item — Flynn siblings whose baptism/confirmation records name Thomas as father would corroborate parentage and identify Patrick's mother, who is entirely absent from the tree
- **`pli_011`** — church (Ireland), FamilySearch, **1830–1845**: required parents' marriage item; Thomas and wife married in Ireland ca. 1844 or earlier, before Irish Catholic civil registration (1864); if a wife's name is identified in pli_010 first, add it as a parameter; supplies the mother's maiden name, which no Pennsylvania source has given
- **`pli_012`** — land, Schuylkill County PA, FamilySearch, **1845–1905** (fallback for pli_009): deeds naming Thomas Flynn as grantor or Patrick as grantee receiving land from Thomas supply collateral parentage evidence; boundary recitals also name adjoining landowners as a FAN source

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Patrick was born ca. 1845 in Ireland (per the 1850 and 1860 census), so Thomas and his wife married in Ireland ca. 1844 or earlier. Irish Catholic civil registration did not cover marriages until 1864, so the record, if extant, would be in Catholic parish registers. FamilySearch holds indexed Irish Catholic parish records for many counties. Without knowing Thomas's county of origin, the search must run broadly on the Flynn surname; if the church records search (pli_010) identifies a wife's given name before this item runs, add her name as a search parameter. Note: this record alone does not place Patrick with the couple — the census household evidence already in hand provides that connection. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

The lifecycle was handled correctly: pl_002 was set to 'superseded' without modifying its items (audit trail preserved), a new plan pl_003 was created with status 'active', and exactly one active plan now exists for q_001. The skill did not create a duplicate plan or leave two active plans. The prior plan items remain intact as the record of what was done.
